lesson.title: Relatives in All Cases
lesson.subtitle: den and dem: the case comes from the relative clause's own verb — whom proves it

hook.title: Whom Still Works Here
hook.content: The man whom I see. The friend whom I gave it to. English's whom is dying at the street level — but it is exactly the case machine German's relative pronouns still run. The case of the relative pronoun comes from ITS OWN clause: the film that I see — the film is the thing SEEN, so German says den (accusative): der Film, den ich sehe. The man I help — helping goes TO someone (the dative club from topic 20), so dem: der Mann, dem ich helfe. The relative pronoun doesn't take orders from the noun it points at; it takes orders from the verb of its own clause.

footnotes.title: The Case Interview
footnotes.content: To find the relative pronoun's case, ask: what job does it do INSIDE the relative clause? Subject of sehe? nominative (der/die/das). Direct object? accusative (den/die/das). Receiver? dative (dem/der/dem). The noun outside decides gender and number; the clause inside decides case. Two interviews, one pronoun.

pattern.title: The Case Roster
pattern.content:
Nominative (subject): Der Film, der gefällt? — keep it simple: der Mann, der kommt. Accusative (direct object): der Film, den ich sehe; die Frau, die ich sehe (die serves both nominative and accusative — feminine didn't split); das Kind, das ich sehe. Dative (receiver): der Mann, dem ich helfe; die Frau, der ich helfe (feminine dative is der!); dem Kind, dem ich das Buch gebe — the double-object verb from topic 20, giving the thing (das Buch, accusative) to the receiver (dem, dative). The basement rule holds through every case: the clause verb waits at the end.

Alongside relative clauses, formal German links two nouns with Genitive possession ('of the'): masculine and neuter nouns use 'des' + noun-s (das Haus des Freundes, der Name des Lehrers), while feminine and plural nouns use 'der' (die Tür der Schule). Prepositions like 'trotz' (despite), 'wegen' (because of), and 'während' (during) also call for this genitive frame.
pattern.linguist_note: whom ↔ wen/wem: English's wh-family (who/whom/whose) is the same interrogative-relative system as German wer/wen/wem. whom kept the accusative -m; German's dem/ihm wear the same ancient dative -m ending. The case is older than both languages' differences.

exercises.prompt: The case roster — match each relative clause with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: the child I give the book to
matching_pairs.german: das Kind, dem ich das Buch gebe

exercises.target_answer: der Film, den ich sehe, der Mann, dem ich helfe, die Frau, die ich sehe, das Kind, dem ich das Buch gebe, der Freund, den ich sehe, die Person, die freundlich ist, der Lehrer, dem ich helfe
exercises.meaning: accusative and dative relatives in action
exercises.explanation: sehen acts ON (den, accusative); helfen and geben give TO (dem, dative). The clause's verb sets the case.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'der Film, DEN ich sehe'?
options: The film is the subject of the clause
The film is the OBJECT of see — accusative job
exercises.target_answer: The film is the OBJECT of see — accusative job
exercises.explanation: The relative pronoun plays the object role inside its clause: der Film, den ich sehe — 'which I see', with whom's case logic.

exercises.prompt: The dative club strikes again: 'Der Mann, _____ ich helfe.' (I help):
exercises.meaning: Der Mann, dem ich helfe = the man I help
exercises.explanation: helfen is a dative verb — helping goes TO someone — so the relative pronoun takes dative: dem.

exercises.prompt: Which English pronoun still wears the accusative case-marking that 'den' carries?
exercises.explanation: whom, wen, wem, ihm, dem all share the ancient -m case ending. English retired whom; German still clocks in daily.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the German sentence you hear:
exercises.target_answer: Der Film den ich sehe ist gut
exercises.meaning: Der Film, den ich sehe, ist gut

vocab_hints.note: the film is being seen — object job inside the clause

exercises.explanation: sehe closes the relative basement; ist holds position 2 of the main clause — two verbs, two floors, one case interview passed.
exercises.spoken: Der Film den ich sehe ist gut
cues: Meaning: "Der Film, den ich sehe, ist gut"
Opens with "Der Film" and ends with "gut".

summary.outcome: Build accusative and dative relative clauses, deriving the case from the clause's own verb.

use_example.german: Der Mann, dem ich helfe, liest das Buch, das ich sehe.
use_example.english: The man I help is reading the book that I see.

summary.takeaway: Gender from the noun outside, case from the verb inside: den for objects, dem for receivers — whom's living twin.
summary.curiosity_teaser: This relative branch ends here — more side paths wait on the map, and the whole compendium waits in review.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Relatives in All Cases (Der Film, den ich sehe, ist gut):
twist.target_answer: Der Film den ich sehe ist gut
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Film den ich sehe ist gut" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Relatives in All Cases without relying on short-term echo.

film.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English film — a direct English loan into German. [wiktionary]

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

sehen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *sehwaną — the identical twin of see (and gesehen ↔ seen); initial s voiced before vowels. [wiktionary]

helfen.etymology_derivation: p → f. Governs the dative case (mir).

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

freund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frijōndz, 'the loving one' — the exact twin of English friend. [wiktionary]

freundlich.etymology_derivation: Freund (friend) plus -lich; the whole compound is documented back to Proto-Germanic *frijondlikaz, matching English friendly part for part, and the -lich suffix is the same element as English -ly. [wiktionary]

lehrer.context_phrase: Der Lehrer kommt in die Klasse.
lehrer.context_translation: The teacher comes into the class.
lehrer.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of lehren (teach) + -er; lehren is cognate with English learn/lore. [wiktionary]

person.context_translation: I do not know this person.
person.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German persōn, the same Latin loan as English person. [wiktionary]

niesen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German niosan, from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną, a variant of *fneusaną. English sneeze is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

vorname.context_translation: Her first name is Maria Keller.
vorname.etymology_derivation: vor + Name, the exact calque of English forename. [wiktionary]

brief.context_phrase: Ich schreibe einen Brief an Oma.
brief.context_translation: I am writing a letter to Grandma.
brief.etymology_derivation: From Latin breve, the neuter of brevis, short, first for a short papal document; the page lists English brief as a cognate borrowed from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
